{"id": "75:31/q12", "question": "How does the verse connect with other parts of the sūra?", "turns_on": "Which earlier motif or scene the verse is read as fulfilling.", "positions": [{"id": "75:31/q12/p1", "position": "It exposes the resurrection-denier foreshadowed by the questions about bones, the Hour and being left aimless.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites 75:3 and 75:36; al-Rāzī adds 75:6. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says denial of the Last Day explains his prayerlessness and connects to the bones question."}, {"id": "75:31/q12/p2", "position": "It belongs to the Resurrection scene announced by the opening oath and the preceding death scene.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī cites 75:1 and 75:29–30: the denunciation reports the person's condition in the afterlife."}, {"id": "75:31/q12/p3", "position": "It identifies the deeds sent ahead or left behind in 75:13.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī identifies disbelief and turning away as one side, delayed faith and prayer as the other."}, {"id": "75:31/q12/p4", "position": "It explains the person's self-witness and attempted excuses in 75:14–15.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī links lack of inward belief and outward action to 75:14, and failure to pray and turning away to the later offered excuses in 75:15."}, {"id": "75:31/q12/p5", "position": "His preference for immediate life in 75:20–21 explains the denial and neglect.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says love of worldly life and abandonment of the afterlife cause these faults."}, {"id": "75:31/q12/p6", "position": "His conduct places him with the grim-faced people, not the radiant faces of 75:22–25.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says belief and prayer would have joined him to the radiant group."}]}
{"id": "75:31/q13", "question": "What consequence does the verse imply for repentance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:31/q13/p1", "position": "His repentance at this stage is useless because he did not accept truth or pray for enlightenment in life.", "reasons": "Asad says the supplied statement completes the sequence and grounds it in 4:17–18."}]}
{"id": "75:31/q14", "question": "How is the lām of ṣallā pronounced in the transmitted readings?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding emphatic sound, the imāla, or the verse ending governs lām's pronunciation.", "positions": [{"id": "75:31/q14/p1", "position": "It is pronounced emphatically after the vowelless ẓāʾ or other triggering preceding letter.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī attributes the emphatic lām after vowelless ẓāʾ to Warsh via al-Azraq; some transmitters retain emphasis before an imāla-bearing alif because of the preceding trigger."}, {"id": "75:31/q14/p2", "position": "It is softened in the specified environments, including before an imāla-bearing alif.", "reasons": "Some Warsh transmitters soften after ẓāʾ with ṭāʾ as in the common reading; al-Hidāya distinguishes open and vowelless ẓāʾ. Al-Mujtabā and al-Taysīr report softness before imāla because of the imāla."}, {"id": "75:31/q14/p3", "position": "Both emphatic and softened lām are transmitted before an imāla-bearing alif.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says several sources preserve both modes."}, {"id": "75:31/q14/p4", "position": "It is softened at verse endings but emphatic elsewhere.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī prefers this distinction: euphony favors softness at endings, the preceding trigger emphasis elsewhere. He lists 75:31, 87:12, 87:15 and 96:10 among verse-final examples, and yaslā al-nār as non-final."}]}
{"id": "75:31/q15", "question": "Is lā here a negative particle or a conjunction?", "turns_on": "Whether the negative clauses can also be treated as coordinated.", "positions": [{"id": "75:31/q15/p1", "position": "It is negative, and the second lā is independently negative.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says a conjunctive reading would resemble supplication, citing grammarians' rejection of 'I struck Zayd, not I struck Amr.' Makkī likewise calls the second lā independently negative."}, {"id": "75:31/q15/p2", "position": "The clauses may be coordinated while retaining their negative force.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya paraphrases them as fa-lam yuṣaddiq wa-lam yuṣall and says fa-lā coordinates the verbs. Al-Samīn asks why coordination must be denied."}]}
{"id": "75:32/q01", "question": "How is ولكن construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q01/p1", "position": "It begins a coordinated corrective clause; the lightened لكن is an inceptive conjunction and does not govern case like إن.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr coordinates ولكن كذب with فلا صدق and observes that the lightened conjunction commonly follows wāw."}]}
{"id": "75:32/q02", "question": "Why add ولكن كذب after the preceding failure to affirm?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding ṣaddaqa means affirmation or almsgiving, and whether lack of affirmation already entails explicit denial.", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q02/p1", "position": "It adds active denial to mere failure to affirm, correcting an inference of silence, doubt, or lesser neglect.", "reasons": "Samīn says many Muslims fail to give or pray without denying, so the clause identifies rejection and aversion as the cause; he calls a reading of the first denial as rejection of the Messenger weak because it would repeat كذب with لكن between equivalents. Biqāʿī says lack of affirmation is not denial and describes persistent rejection overcoming original sound nature. Bursevī puts doubt between belief and denial. Ālūsī rules out silence or hesitation. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says open denial is harsher than nonaffirmation, and turning away broader than omission of prayer."}, {"id": "75:32/q02/p2", "position": "It reinforces or clarifies the preceding negation by stating its contrary.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives two functions of لكن: reinforcement by the contrary, citing 33:5, and clarification of a general negation, citing 33:40."}, {"id": "75:32/q02/p3", "position": "It contrasts denial with an earlier failure to give alms and pray.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers taking ṣaddaqa as almsgiving, supported by 74:43–44; on that reading this verse adds denial instead of merely reinforcing an earlier denial."}, {"id": "75:32/q02/p4", "position": "It restates and intensifies the preceding lack of belief and prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the two failures are restated as active denial and aversion: public denial is worse than nonaffirmation, while aversion exceeds simply not praying. His Ḥalaqāt account calls the pair reinforced restatements and connects each to a separate warning in 75:34–35."}]}
{"id": "75:32/q03", "question": "What did he deny?", "turns_on": "The object understood for the unexpressed object of كذب; several sources name more than one object.", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q03/p1", "position": "He denied the Qur'an, God's Book, or the truth conveyed by it.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī's Basīṭ, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and Qatāda in al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Durr specify the Qur'an or God's Book. Al-Māwardī reports this as one reading. Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Bayḍāwī, and Asad say truth; al-Biqāʿī says God's message. Bursevī includes what was conveyed about the Qur'an. Al-Ṭabrisī's Qatāda includes the Messenger too. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Qur'an's true call and its beliefs; Study Quran says he failed to affirm its revelation. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes the Qur'an. Al-Kur'an Yolu includes revelation and truth, and calls the refusal deliberate lying; al-Iṣlāḥī contrasts denial with the affirmation due to the Messenger and Hereafter."}, {"id": "75:32/q03/p2", "position": "He rejected the Messenger, his message, or his invitation.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz say message; al-Māwardī reports a reading that he called the Messenger a liar. Al-Kashshāf says he disbelieved in the Messenger. Al-Ṭabrisī's Qatāda names Book and Messenger together; al-Qurṭubī counts failure to believe the Messenger among four faults. Abū Ḥayyān says he rejected what the Messenger brought, and Bursevī includes what was conveyed about him. Ibn ʿĀshūr names Muhammad's message; Elmalılı names God, Messenger, Qur'an, and afterlife. Al-Iṣlāḥī says they should have affirmed the Messenger and Hereafter. Kur'an Yolu names the Prophet and says he lies about truth and its messenger; Study Quran says Muhammad's prophethood went unaffirmed. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says denial strikes at the Messenger and all pillars of faith."}, {"id": "75:32/q03/p3", "position": "He denied resurrection or the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr names resurrection alongside the Qur'an and Muhammad's message. Elmalılı includes the afterlife among the objects of denial. Al-Iṣlāḥī says he denied the Hereafter despite the required affirmation. Al-Sāmarrāʾī connects this denial to his question about the Hour in 75:6 and the gathering of bones, calling belief in the Last Day central. Kur'an Yolu puts resurrection among the proofs he resists."}, {

{"id": "75:32/q04", "question": "From what did he turn away?", "turns_on": "What object is supplied to the verb and whether the stress is on faith, obedience, the Messenger, or attention to revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q04/p1", "position": "He turned away from faith or belief.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī in both works, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and al-Ṭabrisī's Qatāda say faith. Al-Kashshāf describes disbelief in the Messenger before the man's departure. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says he denied the call; al-Iṣlāḥī contrasts denial and aversion with the faith due from him."}, {"id": "75:32/q04/p2", "position": "He turned away from obedience, worship, or prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, his Qatāda report, and al-Māwardī's Qur'an reading name obedience; Qatāda in al-Durr says the same. Rāzī says abandonment of prayer merits blame and punishment. Al-Kur'an Yolu says he avoids worship; al-Sāmarrāʾī links aversion to neglected prayer and outward action."}, {"id": "75:32/q04/p3", "position": "He turned away from the Messenger or the One who sent him.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports the latter alongside calling the Messenger a liar. Abū Ḥayyān and Bursevī name the Messenger."}, {"id": "75:32/q04/p4", "position": "He refused the invitation to attend to the Qur'an or truth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies the invitation to examine and reflect on the Qur'an. {"id": "75:32/q06", "question": "What moral contrast does the pair of actions express?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of the paired conduct the source draws out: inward and outward failure, active wrongdoing plus neglected duties, or wilful arrogance.", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q06/p1", "position": "Inward rejection is joined to outward neglect of righteous action.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls the denial inward and the aversion outward, leaving neither inward nor outward good. Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes inward assent from belief and denial expressed by heart, speech, and limbs: he lacked inward faith, openly denied, and abandoned action (75:14). Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pairs rejection of the Qur'an's beliefs with failure to perform ṣalāt, the central pillar of worship. Al-Qurṭubī lists four faults: failure to believe the Messenger, failure to pray, denial, and aversion from prayer. Rāzī similarly joins denial of faith's fundamentals to prayer's abandonment."}, {"id": "75:32/q06/p2", "position": "The two acts are positive wrongs alongside the neglected goods of faith, prayer, and giving.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī counts denial and aversion as two sins; wrongful action and neglected good both provoke reproach, recalling 75:2. Al-Iṣlāḥī says prayer and spending in God's way are the two deeds that would provision the demanding journey; both rest on firm belief in the Hereafter and are the sharīʿah's primary deeds. Elmalılı says he neither affirmed the Hereafter nor worked for God, gave no alms or prayer, then denied and turned away. Rāzī says omitting prayer merits blame and punishment just as unbelief does."}, {"id": "75:32/q06/p3", "position": "He wilfully and arrogantly refuses the truth despite its proofs.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu invokes the proofs of God's unity, resurrection, and punishment, then describes deliberate lying, refusal to listen fairly, blind bigotry, stopped ears, and a locked heart. Al-Iṣlāḥī says reminders of duty meet an arrogant, conceited departure. Al-Kashshāf says he returns to his people strutting after disbelief and aversion."}]}
{"id": "75:32/q07", "question": "How does this conduct connect with the sūra's earlier account?", "turns_on": "Which earlier passage explains or anticipates the two acts and their outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "75:32/q07/p1", "position": "It follows his preference for sin and immediate life and his doubt about resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī links his desires and continued sinning to 75:5, his lack of resurrection belief to his question about the Hour in 75:6, and his denial to the earlier question about gathering bones. He also says love of immediate life over the afterlife in 75:20–21 explains denial and aversion. Elmalılı says the fā joins these clauses to the sinner's worldly pleasure, resurrection question, and eventual return to God."}, {"id": "75:32/q07/p2", "position": "His deeds are what he sent ahead and what he left undone, and he will confront them.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī links 75:13 to disbelief and aversion sent ahead and delayed faith and prayer left behind. He links 75:14 to the discrepancy between absent inward assent, open denial, and action abandoned; he links 75:15 to later excuses when questioned about failure to pray and turning away."}, {"id": "75:32/q07/p3", "position": "Belief and prayer would have placed him among radiant faces; denial and aversion place him among grim faces.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the two groups in 75:22–25."}]}

{"id": "75:33/q05", "question": "What does يَتَمَطَّىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the bodily extension is an affected walking gait or a lazy stretch; both can express arrogance.", "positions": [{"id": "75:33/q05/p1", "position": "He struts or swaggers proudly, with an affected gait.", "reasons": "Muqatil associates such walking with Banu al-Mughira; Zayd ibn Aslam and later transmitters with Banu Makhzum. Ibn Abbas calls it conceit or proud strutting. Al-Tabari, al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and others describe twisting or swaying the back; al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur note lengthened steps. Ibn Kathir adds gloating, insolence, laziness and lack of purpose. Bursevi says he boasts of denial; Biqai says he should have shown shame and humility. Al-Qurtubi explains the gait as stretching and twisting the back; al-muṭayṭāʾ is also described as swinging or extending the arms."}, {"id": "75:33/q05/p2", "position": "He stretches himself lazily or heavily, a gesture of disregard and arrogance.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi says the word can describe stretching on rising from sleep. Al-Jishumi specifies stretching the belly from laziness. Al-Qurtubi stresses disregard; al-Majma' as quoted by Tabataba'i calls it lazy bodily stretching. Al-Samin says he may have begun stretching himself."}]}
{"id": "75:33/q06", "question": "From what is يَتَمَطَّىٰ derived?", "turns_on": "The proposed root: back, stretching with consonant substitution, an ultimate dāl in madd, or maṭw.", "positions": [{"id": "75:33/q06/p1", "position": "From al-maṭā, the back, which the strutter twists or arches.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari, Zayd ibn Aslam and many others connect the word to the back and its proud twisting or swaying. Bursevi specifies an alif substituted for wāw. Al-Majma', quoted by Tabataba'i, traces even lazy stretching back to arching the back. Al-Qurtubi mentions thick basin water called al-muṭīṭa because it spreads or stretches."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p2", "position": "From yatamaṭṭaṭ or maṭṭ, stretching; a strutter extends his body or steps.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares the consonant change with yataẓannā from yataẓannan. Al-Tha'labi says an emphatic consonant becomes yāʾ; al-Nasafi and al-Samin say this avoids three like consonants, al-Samin adducing taẓannaytu, qaṣṣaytu aẓfārī and a verse with taqaḍḍī. Al-Razi compares taqaṣṣā from taqaṣṣaṣa. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Ashur, Bursevi and Biqai explain the stretched stride; al-Samin says this root yields a sense close to the back derivation. Al-Qurtubi and al-Samin compare thick basin water whose name reflects spreading or extension."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p3", "position": "Ultimately from madd, extending, with the root consonant originally dāl.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says maṭṭ and madd share a sense and pictures extending a hand while swaggering; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits this, and al-Jishumi also traces belly stretching to madd. Ibn al-Jawzi notes al-muṭayṭāʾ as the related gait."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p4", "position": "From maṭw, stretching oneself.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites a report of Abu Bakr passing Bilal while Bilal stretched in the sun as usage for the sense."}]}

{"id": "75:34/q01", "question": "What does awlā laka mean as a warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the idiom is heard as a curse, approaching harm, deserved punishment, an elliptical expression, or an ironic predication of his conduct; Iṣlāḥī explicitly disputes the 'befitting' rendering.", "positions": [{"id": "75:34/q01/p1", "position": "A menace or curse: woe to you, may the hated calamity befall you.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls it a fixed warning, comparing 47:20; his anonymous poet, al-Khansāʾ, a line addressed to Aws, and a poem cited by Qurtubī repeat awlā as a threat.
